TRANSCRIPT OF PROCEEDINGS
THE HON CATHERINE HOLMES AC SC, Commissioner
THE ROYAL COMMISSION INTO THE ROBODEBT SCHEME
FRIDAY, 27 JANUARY 2023 AT 10.09 AM (AEST)
DAY 26
MR JUSTIN GREGGERY KC, Senior Counsel Assisting
MR ANGUS SCOTT KC, Senior Counsel Assisting
MS RENEE BERRY, Counsel Assisting
MR DOUGLAS FREEBURN, Counsel Assisting
MS DOMINIQUE HOGAN-DORAN SC, for the Commonwealth
MR TRENT GLOVER, for the Commonwealth
MS ANASTASIA NICHOLAS, for the Commonwealth

COMMISSIONER: Mr Scott, you are appearing with Ms Berry?
MR SCOTT: I am for today's proceedings.
COMMISSIONER: And, Ms Hogan-Doran, you are appearing.
MS HOGAN-DORAN: Commissioner, I appear with Mr Glover and Ms Nicholas for the
Commonwealth. And I will be in and out.
COMMISSIONER: Thanks. I understand you are calling Ms Fredericks first?
MR SCOTT: Yes, Commissioner. The order will be Ms Fredericks, Ms Lumley and then Ms
Essex.
COMMISSIONER: Just for the record, the hold-up was just while Ms Fredericks was being
given the chance to look at some documents, I understand?
MR SCOTT: Yes, Commissioner.
COMMISSIONER: Right. Thanks.
MR SCOTT: Before Ms Fredericks is called, may I tender the exhibits for today's proceedings
which are numbered on a list, I understand, is being provided to your associate,
Commissioner. They should be Exhibits 4131 to 4205.
MS HOGAN-DORAN: Commissioner, can I just confirm that's the exhibit list version 6? It
should have the updated status of claims.
COMMISSIONER: That's the one I'm looking at. 4131, you said?
MR SCOTT: Yes, Commissioner, it skips over - we've got some other evidence but that's - that
will be corrected once that evidence is called later in the proceedings.
COMMISSIONER: Right. Over to 4205.
MR SCOTT: Yes, Commissioner.
COMMISSIONER: Those exhibits are admitted with the numbers they bear.
<EXHIBITS 4131 TO 4205 TENDERED AS PER THE EXHIBIT LIST
MR SCOTT: Thank you. Commissioner, I call Anna Fredericks.
COMMISSIONER: Thanks. Ms Fredericks, will you take an oath or an affirmation?

<ANNA JANE FREDERICKS, AFFIRMED
COMMISSIONER: Thank you. Take a seat. Yes, Mr Scott.
<EXAMINATION BY MR SCOTT KC
MR SCOTT: Thank you, Commissioner. Ms Fredericks, could you please inform the
Commission your full name?
MS FREDERICKS: Anna Jane Fredericks.
MR SCOTT: And you received a notice to give a witness statement and produce documents
dated 18 October 2022?
MS FREDERICKS: That's correct.
MR SCOTT: And you produced a statement in response to that notice dated 21 October
2022?
MS FREDERICKS: That's correct.
MR SCOTT: Are the contents of that statement true and correct to the best of your
knowledge and belief?
MS FREDERICKS: They are.
MR SCOTT: Is this right, Ms Fredericks: You presently hold a position of Principal Legal Officer
at the Department of Finance?
MS FREDERICKS: That's correct.
MR SCOTT: Your statement is principally concerned with a draft advice provided by Clayton
Utz dated 14 August 2018?
MS FREDERICKS: Yes.
MR SCOTT: At the time of that advice, you were employed as a Principal Legal Officer of the
Social Securities and Family sections at the Legal Services Branch at the Department of Social
Services?
MS FREDERICKS: I was, yes.
MR SCOTT: Were you previously employed at the Department - previous to that time, I think,
were you previously employed at the Department of Human Services?

MR SCOTT: What was the period that you were employed at the Department of Human
Services?
MS FREDERICKS: Approximately March 2016 to September 2017. I was an Executive Level 1
lawyer, for periods acting at the Executive Level 2.
MR SCOTT: Where did you work or what area did you work in at the Department of Human
Services?
MS FREDERICKS: Principally in privacy and secrecy law. So with restructures over time, it
ended up being the Program Advice and Privacy Branch, but I specialised in privacy.
MR SCOTT: Was that in the Legal Services -
MS FREDERICKS: Yes, sorry, Legal Services Division.
MR SCOTT: Who did you report to in that area?
MS FREDERICKS: Maris Stipnieks.
MR SCOTT: Right, and who did he report?
MS FREDERICKS: Varying over time, but for the vast majority of my time, it was Annette
Musolino.
MR SCOTT: Including in January to July 2017?
MS FREDERICKS: Yes, correct.
MR SCOTT: Thank you. During the early period of 2017, were you a lawyer embedded in a
team responding to a Senate Inquiry?
MS FREDERICKS: Correct, yes. We were.
MR SCOTT: That team was led either by Jonathan Hutson or Jason McNamara at various
times?
MS FREDERICKS: Jason McNamara for the period I was involved.
MR SCOTT: Okay. And separately to that, is this right, you had involvement in drafting
responses to the Ombudsman for its inquiry in early 2017?
MS FREDERICKS: Correct. I had some input, yes.
MR SCOTT: And that is the investigation by the Ombudsman into the Online Compliance

MS FREDERICKS: Correct.
MR SCOTT: Thank you. Could the witness please be shown this document. Document ID
CTH.3005.0002.3599. Exhibit 1335. Commissioner, this is one of the new documents. Do you
want a hard copy?
COMMISSIONER: Yes, please.
MR SCOTT: Ms Fredericks, do you accept that's an email from yourself to a number of
persons dated 2 February 2017?
MS FREDERICKS: I do.
MR SCOTT: Cc'ing, amongst others, Jason McNamara.
MS FREDERICKS: Yes.
MR SCOTT: And Michael Robinson.
MS FREDERICKS: Correct.
MR SCOTT: Who is Michael Robinson?
MS FREDERICKS: My recollection is vague, but I believe he was another SES officer working in
the Compliance area called into work on OCI, Robodebt as it had become at the time.
MR SCOTT: Did he also, in addition to Mr McNamara, have involvement in the Department of
Human Services' response to the Ombudsman investigation?
MS FREDERICKS: I believe so. Jason was the primary person overseeing the work, but I
believe Michael had involvement as well.
MR SCOTT: Okay. And you see there that it says:
Hi team,
I've populated my sections of the Ombo outline.
Do you see that?
MS FREDERICKS: Yes.
MR SCOTT: Text is distinguished in blue. Do you see that?
MS FREDERICKS: Yes.

MR SCOTT: And the attachment is ‘Outline of OCI Own Motion Investigation Report – AF’. Do
you see that?
MS FREDERICKS: I do.
MR SCOTT: You have had an opportunity to read this document, that is, this email and the
attachment, this morning?
MS FREDERICKS: Correct.
MR SCOTT: Do you have a recollection, having had that opportunity, of what the document
that is attached to this email is?
MS FREDERICKS: A very vague recollection. I had completely - prior to seeing it this morning,
it wouldn't have come in my memory that I had worked on this. Very vague.
MR SCOTT: What is your very vague recollection?
MS FREDERICKS: I believe it was a document - an internal document going - briefing
document to support responses to initial findings in the own motion investigation, so to
support the Department's response.
MR SCOTT: Do you recall that is a marked up version of a draft outline of the proposed
Ombudsman's report into the Online Compliance Intervention?
MS FREDERICKS: Now that you have raised it, I do, yes.
MR SCOTT: You accept that's what it is?
MS FREDERICKS: I accept that's what is, yes.
MR SCOTT: And the text distinguished in blue constitutes your markings, your proposed
markings on that document?
MS FREDERICKS: Yes.
MR SCOTT: That is, proposed, in effect, response by the Department of Human Services to
the draft outline provided by the Ombudsman; correct?
MS FREDERICKS: Yes, correct.
MR SCOTT: Correct. Thank you. If can go to the next document that forms the part of the
same Exhibit, but Doc ID CTH.3005.0002.3600. It looks more like purple on the screen, but do
we - may we take it that that coloured marking up constitutes your proposed markings?
MS FREDERICKS: Yes.

MR SCOTT: That is, what you were proposing as part of the response by the Department of
Human Services to the draft outline provided by the Ombudsman; correct?
MS FREDERICKS: Correct, yes.
MR SCOTT: Thank you. Now, did you have a practising certificate at the time?
MS FREDERICKS: I did, Yes. Sponsored by the Department - restricted government practising
certificate, yes.
MR SCOTT: Okay. And were you aware of the ethical obligations of a lawyer with respect to
involvement in false representations?
MS FREDERICKS: Yes. Broadly, yes. Yes. Due to my legal education, yes.
MR SCOTT: Right. And, that is, it is incompatible with a lawyer's ethical obligations to
knowingly be involved in a false representation, correct?
MS FREDERICKS: Correct. Yes. Correct.
MR SCOTT: And may we therefore take it that you satisfied yourself of the accuracy of the
proposed response that you had marked up in this document?
MS FREDERICKS: Within the resources I had and knowledge I had at the time, yes.
MR SCOTT: Right. So what were the resources you had at the time?
MS FREDERICKS: So we were in a very small team, being quite hard to respond to a very
high-pressure situation. So general resources you would be aware of. I had access to the
internet, that sort of thing. I didn't have access or knowledge of legal advice being obtained
by other Departments into the development of the Robodebt matter. So at the time I was
working on it, we were not - the knowledge was - we didn't have the knowledge that - of the
use income averaging as a primary source. The focus at the time, from recollection, was that
the primary issue with the program was the data matching and the communication method.
And so that was what we were focusing on.
MR SCOTT: Do you agree the usual way that a lawyer confirms the accuracy of
representations that they are involved in is to obtain instructions from their client?
MS FREDERICKS: That's correct.
MR SCOTT: Did you obtain instructions from anybody in the Department of Human Services
as to the accuracy of what's contained in this document?
MS FREDERICKS: So it was - what I've populated in this document was based on information
we were provided by the client, the Department. We had Master Talking Points, a document

And there was a Matter of Public Importance, which was a document that reports to,
obviously, the Legal Services coordination and we were instructed to rely on those
documents as our primary sources.
MR SCOTT: Right. So there was a Master Talking Points document.
MS FREDERICKS: Yes.
MR SCOTT: It was utilised by the Department in responding to any external inquiry about the
Online Compliance Intervention.
MS FREDERICKS: Correct, correct.
MR SCOTT: And you were under instructions to have regard to that in formulating this
response?
MS FREDERICKS: Correct.
MR SCOTT: And you had instructions that it was accurate?
MS FREDERICKS: Yes, correct.
MR SCOTT: Alright. Can I just call out, please, the second-last coloured bullet point on the
screen commencing with the words, "Nothing has changed". Do you see that there?
MS FREDERICKS: I do.
MR SCOTT: Ms Fredericks. Do you see the words, "Nothing has changed"?
MS FREDERICKS: I do.
MR SCOTT: Did those words come from the Master Talking Points document?
MS FREDERICKS: They did.
MR SCOTT: Do you now accept that those words were inaccurate?
MS FREDERICKS: I do.
MR SCOTT: And in what respect were they inaccurate?
MS FREDERICKS: Broadly - I suppose because they are such a broad statement. At the time,
they were based on the understanding that it was the method - the method of implementing
the debt recovery program that was problematic, rather than focus on the use of income
averaging in the assessment of income over fortnightly periods. And, obviously, with the
elapsation of time, it's quite clear that the process had changed.

MR SCOTT: And do you accept that a fundamental way in which the process had changed
was that, previously, if averaging was to be used at all, it was used as a last resort?
MS FREDERICKS: Yes, correct.
MR SCOTT: Whereas, in circumstances where the Department had failed to contact a
recipient of social security, the default position was averaging was to be used; correct?
MS FREDERICKS: That's my understanding. But not specific.
COMMISSIONER: It was also the fact they were now going back years -
MS FREDERICKS: Yes, yes.
COMMISSIONER: - where before it had been a year at the time -
MS FREDERICKS: Correct. There had been a six-year limitation period prior to this.
COMMISSIONER: And there was also the fact that people were being forced online.
MS FREDERICKS: Yes, correct.
COMMISSIONER: Quite a lot had changed, really.
MR SCOTT: Just on the point about the change from using averaging at the last resort to, in
effect, the default position, when did you become - first become aware of that change?
MS FREDERICKS: Later, when I was working in the Department of Social Services.
MR SCOTT: Right. So you weren't aware of that until then?
MS FREDERICKS: No. No, we had - we - we, Legal Services were - and I believe many people
in Human Services were labouring under the assumption that it was a last resort - it had
continued to be a last resort, or it was communicated to be a last resort and continued to be
a last resort, whether, in fact, that was the case or not.
MR SCOTT: When you say that was communicated, by whom was that communicated to
you?
MS FREDERICKS: In all the documentation I received at DHS working on this, the Program
area, primarily. I couldn't name an individual. But I suppose the messaging that we had
received or the instructions we received was that while people were being encouraged or
directed online to confirm their income, the attempts to contact them by letters - and we
were under the understanding that there were a number of letters and Compliance Officers
would call. It later becomes clear that perhaps calls weren't occurring, and letters were not
necessarily being received. We were under the understanding that there had been a number

of attempts to contact the individual to clarify their earnings and then income averaging
would be used as a last resort with the input of the ATO data.
MR SCOTT: Were you aware that, prior to the change, standard process was to attempt to
obtain information from employers?
MS FREDERICKS: I - I was - I'm aware that that's one of the mechanisms that can be used to
obtain income information, yes.
MR SCOTT: And the Department had available to it extensive compulsive powers to require
employers to provide information?
MS FREDERICKS: Yes, I'm aware of that. Yes.
MR SCOTT: Do you accept that it couldn't, on any sensible view, be regarded as using
averaging as the last resort when those attempts to use those powers or not even use
powers, but attempts to contact employers would not be made?
MS FREDERICKS: I would accept that now, yes.
MR SCOTT: Did it occur to you at the time?
MS FREDERICKS: It did not.
MR SCOTT: Are you - is it the position that you simply accepted what you were told?
MS FREDERICKS: I - I would put that I accepted the veracity of what had been put to me on a
complex program, which I didn't have any background or experience and trying to get across
it in a very short period of time.
MR SCOTT: Alright. Were you aware of any AAT decisions at the Tier 1 level in the first half of
2017 stating to the effect that the use of averaging in the way that it was being used under
the Robodebt Scheme was unlawful?
MS FREDERICKS: I was not. The AAT decisions were dealt with by the Freedom of Information
and Litigation Branch and Program Advice was never consulted on those matters or informed
of decisions or outcomes.
MR SCOTT: Was Mr Stipnieks in any way involved in the Freedom of Information and
Litigation Branch?
MS FREDERICKS: No.
MR SCOTT: Was it his usual responsibilities in any respect to be involved in AAT litigation?
MS FREDERICKS: No.

MR SCOTT: What was his main area of practice?
MS FREDERICKS: So we were responsible for - so Program Advice provided advice to the
programs, like, the broad master programs of Human Services. So Centrelink, Medicare. So
we would - there was an area of the Branch responsible for advising - EL2 lawyers
responsible for the advising on the Health Insurance Act, the Centrelink programs, the
delegations, all of those sorts of things. My part of the Branch was responsible for advising
on privacy and occasionally - on occasion, the secrecy provisions contained in the social
security law and more broadly. So it was more of an administrative law, statutory
interpretation type function.
MR SCOTT: So can I understand your evidence to be that your role and Mr Stipnieks's role
was mainly advising on administrative law matters?
MS FREDERICKS: Correct.
MR SCOTT: Alright. And you would be familiar with the principles of administrative law
relating to the lawfulness of administrative decision-making?
MS FREDERICKS: Yes.
MR SCOTT: Including the principle that requires administrative decisions to be based on
evidence?
MS FREDERICKS: Yes.
MR SCOTT: And you understood, did you, that a fundamental assumption that underpinned
the use of averaging of ATO data is that - or was that the recipient had earned the income
disclosed that data over - in equal amounts over each fortnight.
MS FREDERICKS: Yes.
MR SCOTT: And did you understand that the way in which averaging was being used in the
Robodebt Scheme was in circumstances where there was zero evidence to support the
assumption that that data was being - that that income was being earned in equal amounts
per fortnight?
MS FREDERICKS: Sorry, could you repeat that? Sorry.
MR SCOTT: Did you understand that the way in which the averaging was being used in the
Robodebt Scheme involved there being zero evidence to support the assumption that the
income revealed in that data was earned in equal amounts per fortnight?
MS FREDERICKS: I wouldn't necessarily accept that there was zero evidence. The position
that the Department had taken was that the data matching that had occurred and the
identification of the PAYG data was the basis of the evidence that had indicated to the

MR SCOTT: You accept, Ms Fredericks, that one of the features of a - of the law that justifies
the attachment of legal professional privilege to the advice of government lawyers is their
independence?
MS FREDERICKS: Correct. Yes.
MR SCOTT: And so, therefore, it was part of your role to form an independent view as to the
law and not just accept the position put to you by the Department; correct?
MS FREDERICKS: Yes.
MR SCOTT: So quite independently of what the Department's position was, I'm asking you
what you understood the position to be.
MS FREDERICKS: At the -
MR GLOVER: Commissioner, can I just ask - I just want to assist the witness and also my
learned friend. It's a little unclear to me what time period my learned friend is asking the
question about. He seemed to move from the Ombudsman report, which is still on the
screen, up to AAT Tier 1 reviews.
COMMISSIONER: Fair enough. Are you talking about during the time of the Ombudsman's
report?
MR SCOTT: No, I should be clear, to be fair. Up to the middle of 2017.
MS FREDERICKS: Sorry, could you repeat the question? I was distracted, sorry.
MR SCOTT: Up to the point of the middle of 2017, did you independently reflect on the
question of whether or not there was evidence to support the assumption that the data
revealed - sorry, the income revealed in the AAT data was earned in equal amounts per
fortnight?
MS FREDERICKS: My recollection is that I didn't turn my mind to that, because at that point in
time, my understanding was that the primary - primary deficiency of the program was the
communicative nature moving to online, the lack of human involvement, perhaps the timing
of letters going out right before Christmas, not the actual assessment of income.
COMMISSIONER: Can I just ask a question here. Looking at that document but at page 3602,
if I can get you to go to the bottom of that page under ‘Analysis’, Ms Fredericks.
MS FREDERICKS: Yes.
COMMISSIONER: You will see the last bullet point, which says that the Act refers to
assessing/applying income when it's first earned, derived or received.

MS FREDERICKS: Yes.
COMMISSIONER: Then it goes on to say:
But the practicality is, this isn't always known, and the Department can ignore information or
apply it in the best way available.
Which seems tantamount of saying if the Act doesn't provide for it, we will find another way.
Did that not trouble you as a lawyer? Well, first of all, I suppose I should ask you; do you
agree it does seem tantamount for saying that? The Act doesn't provide for this situation so
we will do what we can with what we've got.
MS FREDERICKS: Yes. I do.
COMMISSIONER: As a lawyer, given that this is the exercise of legislated power by a
Department, doesn't it bother you?
MS FREDERICKS: It does. I -
COMMISSIONER: Did it bother you then?
MS FREDERICKS: I don't have a specific recollection relating to this dot point, but I would
comment that there were perhaps a number of things at the time that bothered me.
COMMISSIONER: Isn't this your insertion? Isn't this the blue -
MS FREDERICKS: Yes, so it's my insertion, pulling material from - so it's not necessarily my
words. I have pulled material from other documents that we've been instructed to populate
this document.
COMMISSIONER: Alright. Thank you.
MR SCOTT: Just to complete the sequence of questions on this topic, Ms Fredericks, would
this be right: You didn't independently reflect at all on what you had been instructed about.
And to be clear, in respect of this document about what you've just been asked by the
Commissioner?
MS FREDERICKS: I would agree that it appears not on the documents. Whether I made
comments in the workplace or verbally and was instructed otherwise - but my recollection at
the time - of the time, I honestly couldn't say, hand on heart.
COMMISSIONER: Was anybody else saying anything about this? What was the general feeling
in the group you were in?
MS FREDERICKS: So when I - I was - okay. Context-wise, for this little team of people, there
was a call to nominate EL1-type officers to go and work on this thing because there was a

response. But the instruction within the Department was that no comment was to be made,
no responses without going through certain levels of clearance. Using the Master Talking
Points. No variation from cleared lines. Certainly people were talking at an individual level.
Whether you would count that as a professional level.
MR SCOTT: Who was talking?
MS FREDERICKS: I would say people - people on the floor in the building were
having - making commentary, but it was largely focused on the - like, the substantive
reaction. I think there was an - initially, there was quite a surprise that there had been such a
reaction to this program. Not necessarily around the legality of the methodology for income
assessment.
MR SCOTT: Did any lawyer at the Department of Human Services express any reservations to
you about the lawfulness of the program?
MS FREDERICKS: Not to me. But I would have not been in those discussions at my level.
MR SCOTT: And I think you mentioned a need to stick strictly to the talking - Master Talking
Points.
MS FREDERICKS: Correct.
MR SCOTT: Except with specific levels of clearance. What levels of clearance?
MS FREDERICKS: It would have involved the Secretary.
MR SCOTT: Kathryn Campbell?
MS FREDERICKS: Correct.
MR SCOTT: And you understood there was a clear direction to stick to those talking points
unless instructed otherwise by Ms Campbell?
MS FREDERICKS: Yes. That's correct. It would have come - I wouldn't have been personally
instructed by her, but it would have come down the chain of SES to us, yes.
MR SCOTT: And as a consequence, you did not feel able - is this right - to form any
independent views about the accuracy of these talks points as a matter of law or fact?
MS FREDERICKS: Correct.
MR SCOTT: Thank you. That document can be taken down. Now, Ms Fredericks, are you
aware of the Australian Institute of Administrative Lawyers?
MS FREDERICKS: I am.

MR SCOTT: Do you recall attending the Institute's conference in July 2017?
MS FREDERICKS: I do.
MR SCOTT: Do you recall a number of other Department of Human Services lawyers
attended?
MS FREDERICKS: Yes.
MR SCOTT: Including Mr Stipnieks?
MS FREDERICKS: Correct.
MR SCOTT: Mr Ffrench?
MS FREDERICKS: Yes. Many of us, in fact.
MR SCOTT: Yes. Do you recall Mr Hanks presented a paper at that?
MS FREDERICKS: I do.
MR SCOTT: Do you recall what he said in that paper?
MS FREDERICKS: Broadly. Very broadly.
MR SCOTT: Do you recall - sorry.
MS FREDERICKS: I couldn't articulate it, but I have a broad feeling for it, yes.
MR SCOTT: Okay. I will take you to a document that might reflect your memory.
MS FREDERICKS: Thank you.
MR SCOTT: Refresh your memory, I should say. But you are aware of who Mr Hanks is, aren't
you?
MS FREDERICKS: I am, yes.
MR SCOTT: He's now a King's Counsel by default, but at the time, of course, he was a
Queen's Counsel?
MS FREDERICKS: Yes, correct.
MR SCOTT: A leading public administrative - public lawyer in Australia; correct?
MS FREDERICKS: Correct.

MR SCOTT: Not infrequently briefed by the Commonwealth, in fact. Are you aware of that?
MS FREDERICKS: I wasn't at the time, no.
MR SCOTT: Okay. You're aware that Mr Hanks is actually the author of a textbook on
constitutional law taught to lawyers in their undergraduate studies. Are you aware of that?
MS FREDERICKS: I wasn't. It was not the textbook used in my law school but, yes.
MR SCOTT: Fair enough. But, in any event, you are aware in any event he was a well-
regarded and respected public lawyer with extensive knowledge in administrative law.
MS FREDERICKS: Of course. I knew he was the keynote speaker at that event, so that would
indicate that he was.
MR SCOTT: Thank you. Can the witness please be shown document CTH.3007.0006.7286.
Sorry, Commissioner, I'm getting the Exhibit number. It's Exhibit 4141. Now, I
appreciate - have you seen this document before today, Ms Fredericks?
MS FREDERICKS: I have not.
MR SCOTT: Okay. Well, I won't test your memory on it.
MS FREDERICKS: Thank you.
MR SCOTT: Especially because you're not a party to it. But as we will - I'm going to ask you
whether it purports to provide some form of record of what Mr Hanks said at that
conference. Alright?
MS FREDERICKS: Yes.
MR SCOTT: So if we - and you can see that - if we call out the email at the bottom of the
page, 20 July 2017, 5.22 pm from Mr Stipnieks. Do you see it says:
Peter Hanks QC's main lecture has commenced and an introductory remarks suggest it will be
quite critical of the Department's actions re OCI.
Do you see that?
MS FREDERICKS: I do.
MR SCOTT: If we call out the next email in the chain. Do you see a later email from Mr
Stipnieks saying:
The main thrust is a suggestion that raising of debts using averaging is not consistent with
the terms of the social security law. Further, that the law provides no scope to put the onus

Do you see that?
MS FREDERICKS: I do.
MR SCOTT: Do you recall Mr Hanks saying words to that effect in the presentation?
MS FREDERICKS: I do. I remember his focus was around the - his opinion at that time that the
Scheme had reversed the onus of proving income or disproving a debt. And that
being - being very critical of that.
MR SCOTT: That it had unlawfully reversed the onus?
MS FREDERICKS: Yes.
MR SCOTT: Thank you.
MS FREDERICKS: Yes.
MR SCOTT: Can we call out the next email in the chain? Do you see that's an email from Mr
Stipnieks at a later time, 6.02 pm, stating these words:
Critical of Ombudsman's report for not questioning whether the process was consistent with
the social security law.
MS FREDERICKS: Yes.
MR SCOTT: Do you see that? Do you recall Mr Hanks making comments to that affect?
MS FREDERICKS: I don't recall those comments, but I don't doubt that that's the case, if
Maris has commented on it.
MR SCOTT: And that report, of course, is the 2017 report?
MS FREDERICKS: Yes, the Own Motion.
MR SCOTT: Yes. If you go to the next email, please. 6.08 pm from Mr Stipnieks:
Critical of Secretary's characterisation of letters as merely clarification letters when
customers are forced to engage or have debts raised against them. Says Secretary's
statement in that regard is implausible. Again suggests the process is not consistent with
social security law. Again critical of Ombudsman's report.
Do you see that?
MS FREDERICKS: I do.

MR SCOTT: Next email in the chain, please. Mr Stipnieks says:
Ended by suggesting that someone should look to test the matter in the Federal Court.
Do you see that?
MS FREDERICKS: I do.
MR SCOTT: If we just bring that section of the email down and continue. You can see at the
top an email from Bevan Hannan. Do you see that?
MS FREDERICKS: Yes.
MR SCOTT: Do you know who Bevan Hannan is?
MS FREDERICKS: I believe Bevan was in the media area.
MR SCOTT: Right. And -
MS FREDERICKS: I believe, but - that's my recollection. I'm not certain.
